section.title: Boaz Redeems Ruth
section.sectionRationale: The fourth act is the legal resolution at the city gate. Boaz confronts the nearer kinsman, who agrees to redeem the land until he learns it means marrying Ruth and raising up the dead man's name, then withdraws. Boaz publicly redeems all that belonged to Elimelech and takes Ruth as his wife, and the elders bless the union. It is one movement in which redemption is secured before witnesses.
section.thesis: At the gate the willing redeemer pays the price the nearer kinsman will not, publicly acquiring both the inheritance and the widow, so that the name of the dead is preserved and a Moabite outsider is drawn into the covenant line under the blessing of the whole assembly.
section.frameNote: Four beats: Boaz convenes the nearer kinsman and the elders; the nearer redeemer withdraws; the sandal seals the exchange; and Boaz redeems Ruth to public witness and blessing.

units.label: Boaz convenes the gate
units.note: the case laid before the elders

verses.text: Meanwhile, Boaz went to the {{gate|gate}} and sat down there. Soon the {{goel|kinsman-redeemer}} of whom he had spoken came along, and Boaz said, “Come over here, my friend, and sit down.” So he went over and sat down.
Then Boaz took ten of the elders of the city and said, “Sit here,” and they did so.
And he said to the kinsman-redeemer, “Naomi, who has returned from the land of Moab, is selling the piece of land that belonged to our brother Elimelech.

I thought I should inform you that you may buy it back in the presence of those seated here and in the presence of the elders of my people. If you want to {{gaal|redeem}} it, do so. But if you will not redeem it, tell me so I may know, because there is no one but you to redeem it, and I am next after you.” “I will redeem it,” he replied.

Then Boaz said, “On the day you buy the land from Naomi and also from Ruth the Moabitess, you must also acquire the widow of the deceased in order to raise up the name of the deceased on his inheritance.”
The kinsman-redeemer replied, “I cannot redeem it myself, or I would jeopardize my own inheritance. Take my right of redemption, because I cannot redeem it.”

Now in former times in Israel, concerning the redemption or exchange of property, to make any matter legally binding a man would remove his sandal and give it to the other party, and this was a confirmation in Israel.
So the kinsman-redeemer removed his sandal and said to Boaz, “Buy it for yourself.”
At this, Boaz said to the elders and all the people, “You are witnesses today that I am buying from Naomi all that belonged to Elimelech, Chilion, and Mahlon.

Moreover, I have acquired Ruth the Moabitess, Mahlon’s widow, as my wife, to raise up the name of the deceased through his inheritance, so that his name will not disappear from among his brothers or from the gate of his home. You are witnesses today.”

“We are witnesses,” said the elders and all the people at the gate. “May the LORD make the woman entering your home like Rachel and Leah, who together built up the house of Israel. May you be prosperous in Ephrathah and famous in Bethlehem.
And may your house become like the house of {{perez|Perez}}, whom Tamar bore to Judah, because of the offspring the LORD will give you by this young woman.”

gate.gloss: The city gate. In an Israelite town the gate was the place of legal business, public witness, and the elders' decisions, functioning as the courtroom and civic center. Boaz settles the redemption there so the transaction is binding, public, and beyond dispute.

goel.gloss: Kinsman-redeemer or guardian-redeemer, the near relative legally responsible to rescue his kin, buy back family land, and raise up a name for the dead. The BSB footnote points to Leviticus 25:25-55. The whole scene turns on who will act as goel: the nearer kinsman refuses, and Boaz gladly takes the role.

gaal.gloss: To redeem, act as kinsman-redeemer, or buy back. The verb behind the noun goel; at the gate the nearer relative first says he will redeem, then withdraws when he learns it includes marrying Ruth and raising up the dead man's name. The same root is used by the prophets of the LORD redeeming His people, Isaiah 41:14.

perez.gloss: Perez, a son of Judah by Tamar, born through another account of levirate duty and unexpected blessing, Genesis 38. The elders bless Boaz's house to be like the house of Perez; the closing genealogy runs Perez to Boaz to David, and Matthew 1 carries that same line on to Jesus the Messiah.

basic.context: Boaz goes to the city gate, the place of legal business, and gathers the nearer kinsman and ten elders as witnesses. He offers the nearer redeemer the chance to buy Elimelech's land, which he accepts, until he learns it also means marrying Ruth and raising up the dead man's heir, at which point he backs out. Boaz then publicly redeems the land and takes Ruth as his wife, and the whole assembly blesses the marriage and prays for many children.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a legal, public scene that shows redemption done rightly and openly. The nearer kinsman is not villainous; he simply will not pay the personal cost, which throws Boaz's willing sacrifice into relief. The removed sandal is an ancient legal custom the narrator explains for later readers. The elders' blessing ties this ordinary marriage to the great line of promise.
basic.originalLanguages: The scene unfolds at the gate, shaar, Israel's courtroom. It turns on the goel, the kinsman-redeemer, and the verb gaal, to redeem: the nearer man will not redeem, but Boaz will. The closing blessing invokes Perez, tying this family to Judah's line and forward to David and Christ.
basic.typology: Boaz redeeming what the nearer kinsman could not is a vivid picture of Christ, who accomplishes the redemption that the law and every other would-be rescuer could not. Boaz pays the full price to gain a bride and preserve a name, foreshadowing Christ who pays everything to win His bride and give us His name.
basic.christ: Boaz is the willing redeemer who counts the cost and pays it in full, unlike the nearer kinsman who spares himself. So Jesus, unlike anyone else who might have saved us, willingly gave up His own inheritance, His very life, to redeem us and make us His own. He publicly, openly secured our redemption, and He brings outsiders like Ruth into the family of God.
basic.god: God is at work through law, custom, and human choices to accomplish redemption. We learn that God brings the outsider into His covenant people, that He preserves the name and future of the seemingly forgotten, and that His purposes advance through public, ordinary, faithful acts, all under His sovereign hand.
basic.crossReferences: Deuteronomy 25 gives the levirate duty behind the scene. Genesis 38 tells of Perez, Tamar, and Judah. And Christ as the Redeemer who wins His bride appears in Galatians 4 and Revelation 5.
basic.oneStory: Redemption is secured at the gate as the willing redeemer pays the price the other would not. Boaz gaining Ruth and preserving Elimelech's name points straight to Christ, who redeems His people at the cost of His own life, welcomes outsiders, and secures the line that leads to David and to Jesus.

context.literary:
Ruth 4 opens as a formal legal transaction and reads like a script for a court scene: an offer stated in verse 4, an acceptance in the same verse, a hidden condition that complicates it in verse 5, a withdrawal in verse 6, an explanatory aside for later readers in verse 7, a symbolic sealing act in verse 8, and a public declaration answered by the assembly's response in verses 9 to 11. Nothing here is left to inference; the narrator wants every step of Boaz's redemption on the legal record.

One deliberate device carries real weight. Boaz addresses the nearer kinsman as my friend, but the narrator could easily have supplied a real name; instead this man passes through the whole scene unnamed, in ironic contrast to Boaz, whose name is about to be fixed forever at the head of Israel's most famous genealogy. The man anxious to protect his own inheritance loses even his name from Scripture, while the man who risked his inheritance to preserve another's name gains an everlasting one.

The scene is bracketed by a double you are witnesses today, verses 9 and 10, framing Boaz's declaration the way an inclusio frames a poem, so that everything inside those two lines carries full legal force. And the elders' blessing in verses 11 to 12 rises in three widening circles, from the two mothers who built up the house of Israel, to prosperity in the local region of Ephrathah and Bethlehem, to the ancient house of Perez, so that a single afternoon's transaction at a small town gate is deliberately set beside Israel's whole founding story.
context.historical:
The city gate functioned as Israel's courtroom, marketplace, and public archive combined, the broad space inside a town's fortified entrance where elders sat to hear disputes and witness transactions, Deuteronomy 21:19 and Amos 5:12; ten elders gathered as a formal quorum gave Boaz's transaction the standing of a fully witnessed legal act rather than a private arrangement two men might later dispute.

The sandal ritual in verses 7 and 8 is related to, but distinct from, the shaming ceremony of Deuteronomy 25:9-10, where a widow removes a reluctant brother in law's sandal, spits in his face, and brands his household the house of the unsandaled. Nothing so severe happens here; the kinsman removes his own sandal without protest or humiliation, which suggests Ruth 4 preserves a related but broader commercial custom for confirming any transfer of property right, not the specific punitive levirate procedure. The narrator's aside, explaining a practice that has already faded by his own day, signals that some years have passed between the events and the writing.

Financially, the nearer kinsman's fear is concrete rather than vague. Buying Elimelech's land was a sound investment on its own, but marrying Ruth meant that any son born to them would legally inherit that land in the dead man's name, not his own, Deuteronomy 25:6, so the money the kinsman spent to acquire the land would ultimately enrich a line other than his. He would be paying to grow someone else's estate at the expense of what he could otherwise leave his own existing children, which is exactly the jeopardy to his own inheritance he names in verse 6.
context.canonical:
The blessing over Boaz's house deliberately recalls Genesis 38, where Judah initially withheld his own duty to give Tamar a husband from his family, much as the nearer kinsman here withholds his duty from Ruth; in both stories a reluctant kinsman steps back and God's purposes advance anyway, through Tamar's boldness in one story and Ruth's in the other, until a son named Perez ties both narratives to the same family line, 1 Chronicles 2:4-5. The elders' blessing is not an idle comparison; it is naming the one previous case in Israel's memory where an irregular redemption produced an unlikely ancestor of Judah's house, and asking that Boaz's marriage bear the same kind of fruit.

The chapter's closing genealogy, verses 18 to 22, matches almost word for word the parallel record in 1 Chronicles 2:9-15, showing that later Israel preserved and valued this exact family line as it compiled its national history centuries afterward. Both lists run from Perez through Boaz to David without a single generation of ordinary judges era obscurity, an editorial choice that keeps the covenant line visible even during Israel's darkest years.

Matthew's Gospel later draws directly on this same list of names, Matthew 1:3-6, and deliberately places Tamar and Ruth alongside the Messiah's more expected ancestors, so that Ruth 4's genealogy becomes one link in a chain the New Testament is glad to make explicit rather than hide: God builds the house of David, and afterward the house of the Messiah, through exactly the unlikely and sometimes irregular unions the world might have overlooked.

hermeneutics.authorIntent: The narrator wants his audience to watch redemption happen by the book, not around it, so that no one could later say Boaz seized Ruth or her inheritance improperly. Every step, the public offer, the fair first refusal given to the nearer kinsman, the witnessed sandal, the double declaration, is included so later readers could verify that David's own great grandfather secured his bride and his land exactly as Israel's law required. The author is also teaching, through simple contrast rather than direct moralizing, that covenant faithfulness sometimes costs what self protection will not pay; the nearer kinsman's reasoning is not wicked, only calculating, and the text lets that calculation speak for itself against Boaz's readiness to risk his own estate for a widow's future. Finally, by ending on witnesses and a public blessing rather than a private wedding, the narrator signals that this marriage belongs to the whole community's memory, preparing his hearers for the reveal, two verses later, that this same community's memory now includes the ancestry of King David himself.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: The mechanics of ancient land law, the sandal exchange, the specific order of first refusal, and the particular levirate obligations named here are described as the custom of Israel's own day and are not binding legal procedure for believers now; no one is required to reenact a sandal ceremony to transfer property. What does carry forward is the principle beneath the custom: that legitimate claims should be honored in their proper order, that redemption should be pursued openly rather than by shortcuts, and that willingness to bear cost for another's good is worth more than technical entitlement. Boaz's example teaches believers to weigh personal advantage against covenant loyalty and to choose loyalty, while the nearer kinsman's example, never condemned outright, still stands as a caution against letting the math of self interest have the final word when someone vulnerable is waiting on the outcome.

debates.question: Why did the nearer kinsman back out once Ruth was included?

views.label: Financial self-protection
views.case: He feared that raising up an heir for the dead would divide or absorb his own estate, since the child would inherit Elimelech's land; unwilling to jeopardize his own inheritance, he declined, sparing himself the cost.

views.label: Unwillingness to take on the whole burden
views.case: Redeeming land was gain, but marrying a Moabite widow and committing to raise a family for another man's name was a heavier, less advantageous duty; he wanted the asset without the obligation.

debates.bearing: Either way his refusal magnifies Boaz's willing, costly love, and points to Christ, who did not spare Himself but paid everything to redeem His people.

debates.question: What is the significance of the blessing invoking Perez, Tamar, Rachel, and Leah?

views.label: Linking Ruth to the covenant line
views.case: By naming the mothers who built the house of Israel and the birth of Perez to Judah, the elders place this marriage within the great promise to Judah, Genesis 49:10, and anticipate the royal line that will come from it.

views.label: Honoring God's pattern of unexpected grace
views.case: Tamar and Ruth were both outsiders or irregular figures through whom God nonetheless advanced His purposes; the blessing celebrates a God who works redemption through unlikely people.

debates.bearing: Both readings point forward: this union stands in the line of promise that runs to David and to Christ, in whose genealogy Tamar, Ruth, and Perez all appear.

study.originalLanguages:
The scene unfolds at the shaar, the gate, a word that names not just a doorway but the civic heart of an Israelite town, the space where legal identity, land, and family names were settled in public view.

Two verbs carry the transaction: gaal, to redeem or act as next of kin, and qanah, to buy or acquire, used side by side in verses 4, 5, 9, and 10. Gaal is the older, family centered word, carrying obligation and kinship; qanah is the ordinary word for any purchase. By using both, the narrator shows that what looks, in economic terms, like an ordinary land purchase is, in covenant terms, an act of family redemption, and neither word alone would say enough.

Strikingly, the technical Hebrew term for a brother in law's duty that governs Deuteronomy 25:5-10 never appears in this chapter at all. Ruth's obligation is described only in the vocabulary of the goel, kinsman-redeemer, and the verb gaal, even though raising up an heir for a dead man is exactly the concern that older, narrower word was built to address. The author has quietly widened redeemer language to cover an obligation the law had assigned to a specific relative, showing that Boaz's action, while it answers to levirate custom in substance, is offered and received under the wider, warmer name of redemption.

The chapter is also saturated with shem, name. The nearer kinsman must decide whether to redeem the land so a name will not be blotted out, verse 5, Boaz declares that he acts so the dead man's name will not disappear from among his brothers, verse 10, and twice calls the assembly to witness, using the emphatic phrase you are witnesses today, verses 9 and 10, repetition that functions almost like a legal seal stamped twice for certainty. The chapter that is so concerned with preserving one man's dead name ends, in its final line, by naming David, and the narrator plainly wants his reader to feel the weight of that name landing last.

Finally, Boaz's address to the nearer kinsman, rendered my friend in the BSB, translates an idiom used elsewhere only of an unnamed place, a certain place in 1 Samuel 21:2 and such and such a place in 2 Kings 6:8. Applied here to a person, it leaves the one man in the whole chapter who worries about his own name walking out of the story entirely nameless.

typology.type: Boaz redeeming what the nearer kinsman could not
typology.fulfillment: The law could point to the obligation but could not make anyone willing to carry it, which is exactly why the nearer kinsman steps aside once the cost becomes plain. Paul makes the same diagnosis of the law in general, powerless to do in that it was weakened by the flesh, Romans 8:3, and the answer is not a better law but God sending His own Son. Boaz does not amend the law or excuse the kinsman; he simply does, willingly, what the law required and no one else would do, foreshadowing a Redeemer who succeeds exactly where every previous means of rescue reaches its limit.

typology.type: The willing redeemer paying the full price to gain a bride
typology.fulfillment: Redeeming Elimelech's land was a bargain on its own, but taking Ruth attached a lifelong cost the nearer kinsman would not absorb. Boaz absorbs it gladly. Christ's redemption of the church works the same way at a far greater scale: He gave Himself up for her, Ephesians 5:25, not merely purchasing standing before God but committing His whole self to sanctify and keep a bride who could bring Him nothing in return, so that the cost He bore was total where Boaz's was merely considerable.

typology.type: The outsider brought into the covenant line before witnesses
typology.fulfillment: Ruth the Moabitess is not absorbed quietly; Boaz says her name aloud before the elders and all the people, making her inclusion a matter of public record rather than private tolerance. Paul later insists that in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek, and that all who belong to Him are Abraham's seed and heirs of the promise, Galatians 3:28-29, an inclusion the New Testament likewise refuses to keep quiet. Ruth 4 is a small, local rehearsal of a welcome the gospel will make explicit for every nation.

study.christ:
This chapter answers a question the whole book has been quietly asking: who will actually pay to rescue this family. The nearer kinsman represents every good intention that stops short of sacrifice, agreeable in principle and absent in practice, and Scripture is not shy about naming that as the ordinary shape of human redemption offers, willing until the bill arrives. Christ is introduced into that gap by contrast. Where the nearer kinsman first says I will redeem it and then I cannot redeem it, Jesus never reverses His yes; He resolutely set out for Jerusalem, Luke 9:51, knowing exactly what redeeming His people would cost Him, and did not withdraw.

The public shape of Boaz's redemption also anticipates something about how Christ's redemption is transacted. Nothing about Boaz's claim on Ruth or the land happens in secret or by private arrangement between two consenting parties; it happens before ten elders and all the people, on the record, beyond later dispute. In the same way Paul insists that Christ's redemption was demonstrated, publicly, at the present time, so that God is shown to be both just and the justifier of everyone who has faith in Jesus, Romans 3:25-26. The cross itself, a public execution outside a city gate of its own, Hebrews 13:12, is the ultimate answer to a redemption that refuses to remain private.

There is a genuine reversal in who bears the loss. The nearer kinsman calculates that redeeming Ruth will jeopardize his own inheritance, and he is right, it would have. Christ does not calculate this way. He already possessed every inheritance worth having and gave it up anyway, becoming poor so that we, through His poverty, might become rich, 2 Corinthians 8:9. Boaz risks dividing an estate he already held; Christ surrenders an estate no one could take from Him, for people who had nothing to offer Him in return. The willing kinsman at Bethlehem's gate is a true but small shadow of the willing Redeemer who would, centuries later, be born in that same town and pay a debt no lesser redeemer in all of history could settle.
study.god:
God is barely mentioned by direct action in this chapter, and that restraint is itself instructive. He does not appear to move the nearer kinsman's heart one way or another, does not send a sign, does not audibly commend Boaz's choice; He works entirely through Israel's ordinary legal machinery, ten elders, a public offer, a customary sign, freely made decisions on both sides. This is a God who is fully sovereign over outcomes without needing to override anyone's will to secure them, trusting lawful process and human integrity to arrive exactly where His purposes intend.

His justice shows itself in the fairness extended to a man who ultimately says no. The nearer kinsman is not shamed with the spitting and naming of Deuteronomy 25:9-10; he is given the full first right of refusal, allowed to withdraw with his sandal and his dignity intact, and the text records no rebuke against him. God's justice in this scene protects even the party whose choice disappoints the story's hopes, refusing to turn Boaz's righteousness into an excuse for humiliating someone else.

God's care for the forgotten is visible in what the transaction actually accomplishes. Naomi, who described herself as empty in chapter one, and Ruth, a widow with no legal standing of her own, are both folded into full provision through one afternoon's business at a gate, without either woman having to negotiate for herself. The LORD's concern for widows that Israel's law repeatedly states becomes, here, not a legal abstraction but a concrete outcome secured through a willing kinsman.

Finally, the elders and the people bless the union by name, invoking the LORD to make Ruth like Rachel and Leah and Boaz prosperous in Bethlehem, showing that in Israel ordinary people were expected to be conduits of God's blessing to one another, speaking His favor over each other's lives rather than treating blessing as something only priests could pronounce.

crossReferences.note: Boaz had already told Ruth there was a nearer redeemer who must be given first refusal, and promised he would settle the matter without delay. This chapter shows him keeping that exact promise, word for word, the very next morning.

Judah withholds his own son from marrying the widowed Tamar, refusing a duty much like the nearer kinsman's refusal here. In both accounts a reluctant relative steps back and God's line advances anyway, tying Perez's birth in Genesis to Boaz's redemption in Ruth.

The levirate law behind this scene requires a relative to marry a childless widow and raise up an heir, sealed by removing a sandal. Ruth 4 borrows the sandal custom but spares the nearer kinsman the shaming ritual the law prescribes for outright refusal.

The law establishes that land in Israel belongs ultimately to the LORD and may be redeemed by a near relative when a family is forced to sell it. Boaz's purchase of Elimelech's land in this chapter is a direct, concrete application of this statute.

Job's confession that his Redeemer lives and will stand at last upon the earth uses the same word for redeemer that Boaz bears throughout this chapter, showing that Israel already had a theology of a living, personal redeemer well before this scene at the gate.

The LORD calls Himself Israel's Redeemer, the Holy One who helps a people too weak to help themselves. Boaz's redemption of one struggling family gives that title a small, human face centuries before the exile, when Isaiah will proclaim it to the whole nation.

This later record repeats Ruth's genealogy from Hezron to David almost word for word, showing that Israel, generations after these events, still treasured the exact family line this chapter's transaction secured.

Matthew's genealogy of Jesus runs directly through Perez, Boaz, and Ruth, naming Ruth specifically among the Messiah's ancestors. What this chapter records as a local land transaction, the Gospel later reveals as one link in the ancestry of Christ.

Paul declares that in Christ there is no longer Jew or Greek, and that all who belong to Him are Abraham's heirs. Ruth's public, named inclusion into Israel's covenant family at the gate is a small but real preview of exactly this promise.

study.oneStory:
This gate scene is redemption's grammar spelled out precisely so no reader could miss its shape: someone must pay, the payment must be willingly offered, and the outcome must be publicly secured. That grammar traces back to Eden, where God Himself paid the first cost of covering sin, an animal's death for the skins that clothed Adam and Eve, Genesis 3:21, and it will not be satisfied until a far greater price is paid at Calvary.

Between those two points, this chapter sits on the promise line running from Abraham through Judah, through the earlier redemption Tamar forced from a reluctant kinsman, Genesis 38, through this second redemption Boaz willingly performs, and onward to David, whose house will one day receive the promise that his throne would be established forever, 2 Samuel 7:12-13. The willing kinsman here is not a footnote to that promise; he is one of its load bearing joints, and the text takes care to show his transaction was lawful, public, and complete so that nothing about David's ancestry could later be called into question by friend or enemy of Israel's king.

The chapter also previews something of the new creation. A woman from a nation Israel's law had held at arm's length, Deuteronomy 23:3, is publicly welcomed, named, and blessed by the whole town, a small foretaste of the day every nation, tribe, and tongue stands before the Lamb who was slain to purchase them, Revelation 5:9. What happens quietly at one gate in Bethlehem, an outsider brought fully in at real cost to her redeemer, happens on a cosmic scale at the cross, and will be visibly finished when every redeemed nation gathers at the last, a bride made spotless and free.

sermon.title: “So Boaz Took Ruth”
sermon.why: From Begg's series A Study in Ruth, this message expounds Ruth 4:1-13, the transaction at the gate where Boaz redeems the inheritance and takes Ruth as his wife, valuing righteousness and public integrity. A faithful, expository handling of this movement's redemption scene.

quiz.q: Where did Boaz go to settle the matter of redemption?

options.text: To the city gate, the place of legal business and public witness before the elders.
options.note: Ruth 4:1-2 shows Boaz convening the nearer kinsman and ten elders at the gate.

options.text: To the temple in Jerusalem.
options.note: There was no temple yet, and legal matters were settled at the town gate, not a temple.

options.text: To Naomi's house in private.
options.note: Boaz deliberately made it public at the gate, not private.

options.text: To the threshing floor again.
options.note: The threshing floor was the previous scene; the redemption was settled at the gate.

quiz.q: Why did the nearer kinsman refuse to redeem in the end?

options.text: Redeeming meant marrying Ruth and raising an heir for the dead, which he feared would jeopardize his own inheritance.
options.note: Ruth 4:5-6 shows he withdrew rather than risk his estate.

options.text: He did not have enough money to buy the land.
options.note: He first agreed to buy the land; it was the added obligation of marriage and heir that made him withdraw.

options.text: He disliked Boaz personally.
options.note: The issue was cost to his inheritance, not personal dislike.

options.text: The elders forbade him from redeeming.
options.note: The elders were witnesses; the kinsman chose to withdraw himself.

quiz.q: How was the transfer of the right of redemption sealed?

options.text: The nearer kinsman removed his sandal and gave it to Boaz, an ancient sign of confirmation.
options.note: Ruth 4:7-8 explains the sandal custom that made the matter legally binding.

options.text: They signed a written contract.
options.note: The binding sign here was the removed sandal, a recognized custom, not a signature.

options.text: They exchanged money in secret.
options.note: The exchange was public and sealed by the sandal, not a secret payment.

options.text: They swore an oath at the altar.
options.note: The custom was the sandal at the gate, not an altar oath.

quiz.q: What did Boaz declare before all the witnesses?

options.text: That he had bought all of Elimelech's holdings and acquired Ruth as his wife to preserve the dead man's name.
options.note: Ruth 4:9-10 records his public declaration of redemption and marriage.

options.text: That he was giving the land back to the nearer kinsman.
options.note: The opposite: Boaz took on the redemption the kinsman refused.

options.text: That Ruth must return to Moab.
options.note: He took Ruth as his wife into the covenant people, not back to Moab.

options.text: That Naomi owed him a debt.
options.note: Boaz redeemed for Naomi and Ruth's sake; there was no debt claimed against her.

quiz.q: How does Boaz's redemption picture the work of Christ?

options.text: The willing redeemer pays the full price the other would not, winning a bride and preserving a name, as Christ redeems us at the cost of His life.
options.note: Boaz foreshadows Christ, who did not spare Himself to redeem His people, Galatians 4:4-5.

options.text: It shows redemption is cheap and costs the redeemer nothing.
options.note: The whole point is the cost the willing redeemer pays; redemption is never cheap.

options.text: It teaches that outsiders can never be included.
options.note: Ruth the Moabitess is brought in, picturing the welcome of the nations.

options.text: It proves the nearer kinsman was the true redeemer.
options.note: The nearer kinsman withdrew; Boaz is the redeemer who foreshadows Christ.

questions: The nearer kinsman would not pay the personal cost of redeeming; Boaz gladly did. Where is God calling you to costly love rather than self-protection?
Boaz settled the redemption openly, before witnesses. How does the public, finished nature of Christ's redemption give you assurance today?
Ruth the Moabite outsider was drawn into the covenant family and given a new name and future. How does this shape the way you view your own place in God's family?
The elders blessed the marriage and tied it to God's larger promises. How can you learn to see God's bigger purposes at work in ordinary events like a wedding or a workplace decision?
Christ, our Redeemer, did not spare Himself to win us. How does His willing sacrifice move your worship and your obedience this week?

translationNotes.note: Kinsman-redeemer renders goel throughout the chapter, a legal term for the relative who redeems his kin; the BSB footnote points to Leviticus 25:25-55.
The removed sandal was an old Israelite custom for confirming a transfer of right or property; the narrator explains it because the practice had faded by the time of writing.
Rachel and Leah built up the house of Israel, and Ephrathah is the region of Bethlehem; the blessing places Ruth among the mothers of the covenant people.
The house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah, Genesis 38, ties this marriage to Judah's line and forward to the genealogy of David and Christ.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched this session from bible.helloao.org for Ruth 4:1-12. Verse 4 follows the BSB reading you will not redeem it, noted in the source as supported by many manuscripts and versions.
